co_crag_of_fear.blurb: A compact cliff high on the Lily Mountain hillside in the Estes Park valley, at roughly 9,000 feet. Routes are short, no more than about 45 feet, and a mix of bolted sport lines, a couple of top-ropes and a few gear-protected climbs. Grades run from the easy fives into the 5.10s, with the 5.10 range holding about half the routes, so it suits climbers working through the moderates. Parts of the crag face south and east and catch sun through the morning and midday, which can feel hot even up here. It is a small, approachable spot where beginners and families often start, and it sits just off a hiking trail.
co_crag_of_fear.parking_note: Use the roadside parking at the Lily Mountain trailhead on Highway 7, between Estes Park and Lily Lake. Space is limited and can fill, so leave room for other trail users.
co_crag_of_fear.approach: Follow the Lily Mountain trail, mostly level for about three-quarters of a mile. The cliff comes into view just after the switchbacks, a little below the path.

co_bucket_cave_boulder_aka_pumphouse.blurb: One big sandstone block in the Black Wave boulder field on Nine Mile Hill, along the Unaweep Canyon highway near Grand Junction. About ten problems cover a friendly range, mostly V1 and V2 with a handful of V3 and V4 lines. The front side offers good rock with long traverses, vertical faces and slabby moves, while the back side is tall and mixes steep and vertical problems. It is a good stop for a mellow session or for climbers building up through the easier V-grades, and it sits only a short walk from the road.
co_bucket_cave_boulder_aka_pumphouse.parking_note: Use the first roadside pullout for the Black Wave boulders along Highway 141 on Nine Mile Hill. The boulder is a short walk straight down the slope from there.

co_minturn_mile_boulder_the.blurb: A single prominent block in the Klettergarden bouldering area between Minturn and Red Cliff, in the Eagle County mountains at around 8,800 feet. This is the area's hard-problem boulder: ten problems, none easy, running from V4 up through the V6 to V9 range with a few V10 and V11 lines. The east face is overhanging, and a bench faces the problems, handy for resting between goes. The surrounding boulders sit in shady aspen, with good-quality rock, so it makes a pleasant summer and fall destination for strong boulderers.

co_imitation_wall.blurb: A short, shady wall tucked in the trees in the Devil's Gate sector of Devil's Head, in the South Platte country. Ten routes mix sport and trad, with grades from the low fives to 5.10; most lines are all-sport or all-trad rather than mixed. The rock has dark patina, sculpted jugs and some steady cracks, and the face is more vertical than steep. Because it stays shaded most of the day, it works well on hot summer afternoons, and the base is roomy enough for families and newer climbers. A single rack of gear to about a number 3 or 4 covers the trad routes.

co_brother_s_lookout_south_face_the.blurb: The hard-problem sector of Alderfer/Three Sisters Park, in the foothills above Evergreen at about 7,800 feet. Ten boulder problems here run from the V4 range up to the V12 range, with several highballs, and the rock quality is excellent. The main wall faces south and soaks up sun, which makes it a good choice for winter, late fall and early spring days. The park as a whole is a pine forest with lots of trails, so expect hikers on the way in, though the bouldering itself tends to be fairly quiet. Bring plenty of pads.
